body:
## Module 2 in two minutes

Every other role in this curriculum feeds a model material that has a fact behind it. **Your core input is two or more people telling incompatible stories about the same events** — and the incompatibility is not noise around a signal. **The incompatibility is the evidence.**

Which changes the standard. *Accurate to the source* is necessary and has stopped being the test: a summary can be faithful to all three statements and still be worse than useless.

**Ask a model to summarize three conflicting accounts and it will produce something coherent — because coherence is what summarization is.** So:

> **A model can be accurate to every source it was given and still destroy the finding, by producing a coherent account of events that were never coherent.**

Four mechanisms, none of them a hallucination. **Smoothing** — "witnesses described a heated exchange" merges an allegation of shouting, a description of mutual raised voices, and an account of nothing unusual into a characterization nobody gave. **Averaging** — the contested detail lands on the middle version, which is weighing performed invisibly. **Confidence flattening** — "I think it was Tuesday, but I might be wrong" and "it was Tuesday" arrive identically, and the hedge was the most useful word in the sentence. **Narrative completion** — the joins a story needs, supplied and unmarked.

**And this is not 101 M6.** Check the summary against the sources and every sentence holds. There is no fabrication to find.

### The line

> **A model may locate conflicts. Only a human may resolve them.**

**Locating** is factual and checkable in seconds: *A says Tuesday. B says Thursday. The calendar says Wednesday.* Rung two, safe, and genuinely valuable — a systematic pass catches conflicts a loaded investigator misses.

**Resolving** is a credibility determination. Rung four. Easy to avoid, because the sentence announces itself.

**And the request in between, where careful people go wrong:** *"Which account is most consistent with the other evidence?"* That is weighing. It takes conflicts you legitimately located and asks for a ranking against a standard, and a ranking against a standard is a finding. Three more on the wrong side: *does the respondent's account hold together*, *rate each account's reliability*, and *which parts should I be sceptical about*.

The deeper reason the line sits exactly here: **your standard of proof is not a threshold to check a number against. It is an instruction to weigh.** So **a model that weighs has applied your standard of proof on your behalf, and you cannot say how** — leaving you a conclusion, an impression of why, and no reconstructable path from evidence to finding. Which is the one thing the report has to contain, and the first thing the other side attacks.

**Practical form:** conflicts as a list, one per row, exact words at issue, **no commentary.** Compare statements to statements and statements to documents — **never accounts to each other on quality.**

**The full module adds the property that produces the worst outcomes, because it is invisible: silence.**

**An account that omits something is not an account that denies it.** A witness who doesn't mention the 14 March meeting may not have been there, may not remember, may not have been asked, or may be avoiding it. Four completely different evidential states, one identical statement.

And **models fill gaps**, because filling gaps is most of what generative systems do. The completion isn't marked, isn't flagged as inference, and reads exactly like the parts that came from the material. Which makes the omission — often the most important thing in a statement — **the single thing a fluent summary most reliably disappears.** *Nobody mentioned the earlier conversation* is a finding. *The summary doesn't mention it* looks like nothing at all.

So never ask what an account **establishes.** Ask three questions and keep the three answers separate on the page: **what does it contain** (assertions actually made, quoted), **what does it omit** (which matters at issue does it not address), and **what does it contradict** (which account or document, on which point, in whose words). Merging them is harmonization performed by you rather than by the model, and the document is no better for having been assembled by hand.

The check to run on any AI-assisted text before it goes near a file: **does this distinguish what somebody said from what somebody did not say?** If not, it has treated silence as agreement — **and silence is where the case usually is.**
